sections.title: Mental model — choreograph groups, recurse the rest

blocks.md: **Hard list problems = LOCAL rewiring dance + RECURSION for the remainder. Master one group's choreography; the mantra assembles the whole.**

blocks.label: Reverse Nodes in k-Group (LC25)
blocks.py:
def reverse_k_group(head, k):
    check, cnt = head, 0
    while check and cnt < k: check = check.next; cnt += 1
    if cnt < k: return head          # partial tail untouched

    prev, cur = None, head
    for _ in range(k):               # reverse exactly this group
        ahead = cur.next; cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, ahead
    head.next = reverse_k_group(cur, k)   # MANTRA: rest recursive
    return prev

blocks.label: Merge-k preview (LC23) — heap of heads
blocks.py:
import heapq
heap = [(l.val, i, l) for i, l in enumerate(lists) if l]
heapq.heapify(heap)                   # (val, tiebreak, node) triples
dummy = Node(0); tail = dummy
while heap:
    v, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
    tail.next = node; tail = tail.next
    if node.next: heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
return dummy.next                     # N log k accounting

items.title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
items.statement: Section implementation; then iterative connector variant.

solutionCode.label: check k nodes exist FIRST, reverse the block, recurse on the rest
solutionCode.py:
def reverse_k_group(head, k: int):
    # EXISTENCE CHECK FIRST: a trailing block shorter than k stays untouched
    probe = head
    for _ in range(k):
        if probe is None:
            return head
        probe = probe.next
    # reverse exactly k nodes; cur ends at the (k+1)-th
    prev, cur = None, head
    for _ in range(k):
        ahead = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = ahead
    head.next = reverse_k_group(cur, k)   # old head is now the block's tail
    return prev                           # prev is the block's new head

items.complexity: Time O(n) — every node is visited a constant number of times. Space O(n/k) for the recursion, or O(1) for the iterative form.

followups.q: Why must the existence check come before any reversing?
followups.a: The problem says a final block with fewer than k nodes stays in original order. If you reverse first and check after, you have already mutated it and must reverse it back. Probing k nodes costs O(k) and is thrown away only on the last block, so the total stays O(n).

followups.q: Why is head->next the right place to attach the recursive result?
followups.a: After reversing a block, the node that was the head is now the block's tail — it is the only node whose next pointer is still free. prev becomes the new head that gets returned upward. Naming which pointer is which after the flip is where this problem is won or lost.

items.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
items.statement: Solve via k=2 recognition AND standalone pointer dance.

solutionCode.label: k-group with k=2, plus the standalone pointer dance
solutionCode.py:
def swap_pairs_via_k_group(head):
    """Recognition route: this IS reverse_k_group with k fixed at 2."""
    return reverse_k_group(head, 2)


def swap_pairs(head):
    """Standalone iterative route, O(1) space."""
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    while prev.next and prev.next.next:
        a = prev.next
        b = a.next
        a.next = b.next     # a jumps over b
        b.next = a          # b takes a's place
        prev.next = b       # predecessor now points at b
        prev = a            # a is the tail of this pair
    return dummy.next

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) for the iterative form.

followups.q: Why is the three-line rewire in that exact order?
followups.a: a.next = b.next must happen before b.next = a, or you lose the rest of the list. b.next = a must happen before prev.next = b, or a is orphaned. Each line consumes a pointer the next line would destroy — writing them in any other order drops nodes.

followups.q: Which version would you give in an interview?
followups.a: Say the recognition first — "this is k-group with k = 2" — then write the standalone one, because it is O(1) space where the recursive k-group costs O(n/2) stack. Showing the generalisation and then the specialised implementation is worth more than either alone.

items.title: Rotate List
items.statement: k normalized; circular trick or gap-slider.
hints: Advance n−k from head, break there.

solutionCode.label: close the ring, walk n-k, cut
solutionCode.py:
def rotate_right(head, k: int):
    if head is None or head.next is None or k == 0:
        return head
    n, tail = 1, head
    while tail.next:                 # count AND find the tail in one pass
        tail = tail.next
        n += 1
    k %= n                           # k > n is the classic trap
    if k == 0:
        return head
    tail.next = head                 # close the ring
    new_tail = head
    for _ in range(n - k - 1):
        new_tail = new_tail.next
    new_head = new_tail.next
    new_tail.next = None             # cut the ring open
    return new_head

followups.q: Why normalise k with a modulo?
followups.a: Rotating by n returns the original list, so only k mod n matters. LeetCode allows k up to 2*10^9 against a list of 500 nodes — without the modulo you walk four million times per rotation for no effect, and the loop bound n-k-1 goes negative.

followups.q: Why is the new tail at index n-k-1?
followups.a: Rotating right by k moves the last k nodes to the front, so the split falls after the first n-k nodes. The last of those is at index n-k-1 (0-based). Verify on n=5, k=2: new tail at index 2, so [1,2,3] stays and [4,5] moves front — giving 4,5,1,2,3.

items.title: Add Two Numbers II
items.statement: MSB-first inputs; no list mutation allowed? Then stacks.

solutionCode.label: stacks give LSB-first access without mutating the inputs

items.complexity: Time O(m + n), space O(m + n) for the stacks — O(1) if you are permitted to reverse the inputs.

followups.q: Why stacks rather than reversing the lists?
followups.a: Reversing mutates the caller's input, which the problem's follow-up explicitly forbids. Stacks buy LSB-first access for O(n) space without touching the originals. If mutation were allowed, reverse-add-reverse is O(1) space and faster.

followups.q: Why does prepending give the right digit order?
followups.a: Addition produces digits least-significant first, but the answer must be most-significant first. Prepending each new digit pushes earlier (less significant) digits further right, so the final head holds the most significant digit — no reversal pass needed.

items.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
items.statement: Heap-of-heads now; divide-conquer-pairing as alternative — compare aloud.
hints: Pairwise merge = log k passes of LC21.

solutionCode.label: min-heap of the k current heads
solutionCode.py:
import heapq


def merge_k_lists(lists):
    # heapq cannot compare ListNodes, so carry a tiebreaker index
    pq = []
    for i, node in enumerate(lists):
        if node:
            heapq.heappush(pq, (node.val, i, node))

    dummy = ListNode()
    tail = dummy
    while pq:
        _, i, node = heapq.heappop(pq)
        tail.next = node
        tail = node
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(pq, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    tail.next = None
    return dummy.next

items.complexity: Heap: O(N log k) for N total nodes across k lists, O(k) space. Pairwise merge: O(N log k) time, O(1) extra space.

followups.q: Give the N log k sentence.
followups.a: Every one of the N nodes is pushed and popped exactly once, and the heap never holds more than k entries — so each operation is log k. Total N log k. A naive "merge them all pairwise left to right" is O(Nk) because the accumulator is re-walked every time.

Merging lists in pairs halves the count each round, so it takes log k rounds and each round touches all N nodes — also O(N log k), but with O(1) extra space and better cache behaviour since it is just repeated LC21. The heap wins when lists arrive as a stream; pairing wins when you have them all up front.

items.title: Flatten Sorted Linked Lists (GFG)
items.statement: Bottom lists sorted vertically — fold merge pairwise until one.

solutionCode.label: merge on the BOTTOM pointer, fold across the top-level chain

items.complexity: O(N log k) for k lists totalling N nodes when folded pairwise; the simple left-to-right fold shown here is O(N*k) worst case but trivial to reason about.

followups.q: Why must next be cleared on every flattened node?
followups.a: The result is required to be a single bottom-linked list. Leaving stale next pointers means a traversal following next sees a half-flattened structure, and any validator checking "next is null everywhere" fails. It is the part most implementations forget because the bottom walk still looks right.

followups.q: Why fold right-to-left rather than left-to-right?
followups.a: Recursing right first means each merge combines the current list with an already-fully-flattened remainder — one merge per top-level node. Folding left-to-right re-walks the growing accumulator every time, which is the O(N*k) shape. For true O(N log k), pair the lists up like merge sort instead.

items.title: Reorder List

solutionCode.label: split, reverse the tail, zipper the two halves
solutionCode.py:
def reorder_list(head) -> None:
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return
    # 1. FIRST middle, so the second half is never longer than the first
    slow = fast = head
    while fast.next and fast.next.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next

    # 2. reverse the second half and detach it
    prev, cur = None, slow.next
    slow.next = None
    while cur:
        ahead = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = ahead

    # 3. weave: alternate one node from each half
    a, b = head, prev
    while b:
        na, nb = a.next, b.next
        a.next = b
        b.next = na
        a, b = na, nb

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1). Three primitives you already have: find middle, reverse, weave.

followups.q: Why the FIRST middle here rather than the second?
followups.a: The weave drives off the second half and stops when it runs out. Taking the first middle makes the second half equal or shorter, so a always has a node to pair with b. Taking the second middle makes the second half longer and the last weave step dereferences a null a.

followups.q: Why is this worth solving as three named steps?
followups.a: Each step is a primitive you already have — middle, reverse, merge — and each is independently testable. Trying to reorder in a single clever pass is where people lose the thread. Composing known pieces is both faster to write and far easier to defend at a whiteboard.

items.title: Copy List with Random Pointer — revisit under time pressure
items.statement: Re-solve Foundations F023 cold in ≤15 min; narrate O(1)-space interleave.

solutionCode.label: clone after each node, wire randoms by adjacency, then unweave
solutionCode.py:
class RNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None, random=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = nxt
        self.random = random


def copy_random_list(head):
    if head is None:
        return None
    # PASS 1: A -> A' -> B -> B' -> ...
    t = head
    while t:
        t.next = RNode(t.val, t.next)
        t = t.next.next
    # PASS 2: a clone's random is the ORIGINAL random's clone, which sits right after it
    t = head
    while t:
        t.next.random = t.random.next if t.random else None
        t = t.next.next
    # PASS 3: unweave, restoring the original list
    new_head = head.next
    t = head
    while t:
        clone = t.next
        t.next = clone.next
        clone.next = t.next.next if t.next else None
        t = t.next
    return new_head

items.complexity: Interleave: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Hash map: O(n) time, O(n) space.

followups.q: Why does interleaving remove the need for a map?
followups.a: The map exists to answer "given an original node, where is its clone?". After interleaving, that answer is always original.next — an O(1) lookup encoded in the structure itself. The list is acting as its own hash table, which is what buys O(1) extra space.

followups.q: What is the hash-map fallback, and when would you use it?
followups.a: One pass building {original: clone}, a second wiring next and random through the map. It is O(n) space but far harder to get wrong under pressure. Say it first, get it working, then offer the interleave as the O(1)-space refinement — that ordering is worth more than freezing while trying to recall the three-pass dance.
